title: Pairs That Pull Apart
objectives: I can name the opposite of ten words and use each pair in a sentence.
I can use antonyms and synonyms to figure out a word I do not know.
I can show that words such as ancient and old are close but not the same.
I can write about a contest or a change using pairs of opposite words.
rationale: Opposite pairs teach two words at once and give students the antonym and synonym habit that context-clue work depends on. Four pairs anchor the unit (ancient and modern, abundant and scarce, ascend and descend, victory and defeat), and expand and obvious join them so students can compare with a synonym or an opposite. The words cover time, amount, direction, and winning, and they appear together in a narrative so that students must use context to tell which word belongs. Pairs reuse spacious, cramped, and timid from earlier units.

words.def: Very, very old, from a time long ago.
words.ex: Scientists found ancient coins buried near the old city wall.
words.ex2: The ancient oak had stood in the field for six hundred years.
words.nonExample: A toy bought last week is not ancient.

apps.academic: In social studies, we learn about ancient people through the objects they left behind.
apps.spoken: That ancient tree must be hundreds of years old.
apps.writing: Use ancient for things from a very long time ago, not just old things.

cloze.s: The museum's ___ pottery was made by people who lived thousands of years ago.

cloze2.s: Hikers found a ___ cave painting that was older than any city on the map.

misuse.s: The ancient sandwich had been made fresh just five minutes ago.
misuse.why: Ancient means from a very long time ago; a fresh sandwich is new.

visual.alt: An old clay pot in front of stone columns.

words.def: Of the present time; new and up to date.
words.ex: The museum has both ancient pots and modern art.
words.ex2: A modern phone can do more than an old computer.
words.nonExample: A horse and cart from long ago is not modern.

apps.academic: Modern tools often work faster and more safely than the tools people used long ago.
apps.spoken: Our school has a modern gym with a new floor.
apps.writing: Use modern for things that belong to today.

cloze.s: The old house had a ___ kitchen with a new stove and fast dishwasher.

cloze2.s: In the ___ city, tall glass towers stood where small wooden houses once were.

misuse.s: The modern cave painting was thousands of years old and made by people long ago.
misuse.why: Modern means of today; a painting thousands of years old is ancient.

visual.alt: A tall glass city building beside a smartphone.

words.def: Existing in large amounts; more than enough.
words.ex: Fish are abundant in the clear mountain lake.
words.ex2: Apples were abundant that fall, so we gave baskets to our neighbors.
words.nonExample: Three crumbs left in a bag are not abundant.

apps.academic: In science, a habitat with abundant food can support many animals.
apps.spoken: There is abundant food at the picnic, so please eat more.
apps.writing: Use abundant for things that are found in large amounts.

cloze.s: After the rainy spring, wildflowers were ___ in the meadow, and every hill was covered with color.

cloze2.s: Fresh berries were ___ at the farm stand, with baskets stacked up to the roof.

misuse.s: Water was abundant in the desert, where there was only one tiny puddle for miles.
misuse.why: Abundant means large amounts; one tiny puddle is scarce.

visual.alt: A basket overflowing with red apples.

words.def: Hard to find; not enough to go around.
words.ex: Water is scarce in the desert.
words.ex2: During the storm, fresh food became scarce at the store.
words.nonExample: A park full of benches is not a place where benches are scarce.

apps.academic: When a resource is scarce, people must share it carefully.
apps.spoken: Parking spaces are scarce near the stadium.
apps.writing: Use scarce for things that are hard to find or not enough for everyone.

cloze.s: After the long winter, food was ___ for the deer, and they searched for hours to find a few leaves.

cloze2.s: Tickets to the show were ___, and only a few families got seats.

misuse.s: Snow is scarce in the mountains in January, when it falls in huge piles all over the town.
misuse.why: Scarce means hard to find; huge piles of snow are abundant.

visual.alt: A dry desert with one small water drop.

words.def: To go up or climb higher.
words.ex: The hikers ascended the mountain trail slowly.
words.ex2: The balloon began to ascend into the clear blue sky.
words.nonExample: Sliding down a hill is not ascending.

apps.academic: Rockets ascend through the air into space.
apps.spoken: We ascended the stairs to the top floor.
apps.writing: Use ascend for climbing or rising to a higher place.

cloze.s: As the plane began to ___ above the clouds, the city below grew smaller and smaller.

cloze2.s: The climbers had to ___ the steep cliff slowly, one careful hold at a time.

misuse.s: The elevator ascended to the basement, three floors below the street.
misuse.why: Ascend means to go up; going to the basement is descending.

visual.alt: A hot-air balloon rising into the sky with an upward arrow.

words.def: To go down to a lower place.
words.ex: The elevator descended to the basement floor.
words.ex2: The plane began to descend as it neared the airport.
words.nonExample: Climbing up a ladder is not descending.

apps.academic: A parachute slows a person as they descend.
apps.spoken: We descended the stairs to the cafeteria.

cloze.s: After reaching the peak, the hikers began to ___ the trail on the other side of the mountain.

cloze2.s: The divers slowly ___ into the dark water, deeper and deeper.

misuse.s: The kite descended higher and higher until it nearly touched the clouds.
misuse.why: Descend means to go down; going higher and higher is ascending.

visual.alt: A parachute drifting down with a downward arrow.

words.def: To get bigger or make something bigger.
words.ex: A balloon will expand as you blow air into it.
words.ex2: The library plans to expand and add a new children's room.
words.nonExample: An ice cube shrinking in the sun is not expanding.

apps.academic: In science, many materials expand when they are heated.
apps.spoken: The town wants to expand the park.
apps.writing: Use expand for growing in size or amount.

cloze.s: When the baker added yeast, the dough began to ___ and fill the whole bowl.

cloze2.s: The school plans to ___ the cafeteria so that more students can sit down to eat.

misuse.s: The balloon will expand until it shrinks to the size of a pea.
misuse.why: Expand means to get bigger; shrinking to a tiny size is the opposite.

visual.alt: A balloon growing larger with arrows pointing outward.

words.def: Success in winning a game, contest, or battle.
words.ex: The team celebrated its victory with cheers and pizza.
words.ex2: After weeks of practice, her victory in the spelling bee felt well earned.
words.nonExample: Losing a game by a large score is not a victory.

apps.academic: In history, a victory in a battle could change a whole country.
apps.spoken: We shook hands after our victory.
apps.writing: Use victory for winning, and mention how the winner felt.

cloze.s: Fans threw their hats into the air and cheered when the final goal gave the home team a ___.

cloze2.s: Months of practice paid off in a hard-won ___ at the science fair.

misuse.s: The team's victory came when they lost every game and went home without the trophy.
misuse.why: Victory means winning; losing every game is defeat.

visual.alt: A gold trophy with party confetti.

words.def: A loss, when you do not win.
words.ex: The team's defeat in the final game made them sad.
words.ex2: She learned from her defeat and practiced harder.
words.nonExample: Winning the trophy is not a defeat.

apps.academic: In stories, a character often learns something important from a defeat.
apps.spoken: We accepted our defeat and shook hands.
apps.writing: Use defeat for a loss, and show what the character learns.

cloze.s: The soccer team was sad after the ___ in the championship game, and many players cried.

cloze2.s: Even after a hard ___, Leo smiled and said he would try again next year.

misuse.s: The champion's defeat was a happy one because she won every race and took home the cup.
misuse.why: Defeat means a loss; winning every race is victory.

visual.alt: A silver medal next to a sad face.

words.def: Easy to see or understand; plain to everyone.
words.ex: It was obvious from his smile that he loved the gift.
words.ex2: The answer was obvious once the teacher drew a picture.
words.nonExample: A secret hidden in a locked box is not obvious.

apps.academic: A good reader finds the obvious clues in a story and also looks for hidden ones.
apps.spoken: It's obvious that you worked hard on this.
apps.writing: Use obvious for something that is easy to see or understand.

cloze.s: With a muddy trail leading from the door to the cookie jar, the thief was ___ to everyone in the kitchen.

cloze2.s: The sign was so big and bright that the road to the museum was ___.

misuse.s: It was obvious that no one could possibly figure out the secret, because it was hidden from everyone.
misuse.why: Obvious means easy to see; something hidden from everyone is not obvious.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass pointing at a large clear arrow.

passage.title: The Tower Contest
paras: Our class visited an ancient castle that had stood on a hill for nine hundred years. Next to it, the museum was modern, with glass walls and bright lights. Our guide told us that when the castle was built, good stone was scarce, so builders had to carry it from far away.

"Today we will hold a contest," said the guide. "You will ascend the tower steps, count the windows, and then descend again. The first team back with the right number wins." The count was not obvious, because some of the windows were small and hidden behind vines.

My team climbed slowly, counting out loud. On the way down, a boy from the other team tripped on the last step, and we passed him. We reached the guide first with the right number, which was twelve. Our victory felt wonderful. The other team groaned at their defeat, but they shook our hands.
Later we ate lunch in the garden, where apples were abundant. The guide said the town wants to expand the museum so more classes can visit each year.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "scarce" tells us that good stone was
qs.why: Builders had to carry stone from far away, which shows it was hard to find nearby.

qs.q: Why was the guide's question not obvious to answer?
choices: The guide did not ask a question.
Some windows were small and hidden behind vines.
qs.why: The text says some windows were hidden, so it was hard to see all of them.

qs.q: Which detail shows that the museum was newer than the castle?
choices: It was nine hundred years old.
It was modern, with glass walls and bright lights.
qs.why: Modern means of the present time, while the castle was ancient.

qs.q: What is the passage mostly about?
choices: A school trip to a castle where students took part in a contest
How to build a glass museum
A guide who lost a contest
qs.why: Most of the passage describes the visit and the tower contest.

write.frame: Our ___ felt like a victory (or defeat) because ___. It was obvious that ___.

study.task: Match the unit words that are opposites and write the pairs. Then choose three other words and write a synonym for each. Explain to a partner how the pair is the same or different.

Write a sentence about something that is abundant in your home or school.

The team won the game and celebrated its victory with cheers.

What should a team do after a defeat? What should a team do after a victory?
When might something that is scarce become abundant?
produce.explain: Explain the difference between ancient and modern. Use both words and an example for each.

argue.prompt: Claim: It is important to learn about ancient history. Do you agree or disagree? Give two reasons.

constructed.prompt: Write two sentences that compare an ancient thing with a modern thing. Tell what each one is used for.

constructed.model: In a green meadow, food is abundant, so rabbits grow fat. In a dry desert, food is scarce, so animals must travel far to eat.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that sort into opposite pairs and near-opposites, practice finding antonyms and synonyms, and read a narrative where the pairs appear in context. They write sentences that use a pair of opposite words.

notes.va.ancient.adj: Ancient is older than old. Ask students to put old, older, and ancient on a time line. Link to modern as the opposite.
notes.va.modern.adj: Modern is of today. Do not treat new and modern as always the same: a new copy of an old tool is not modern. Keep the focus on time.
notes.va.abundant.adj: Abundant is more than enough. Pair it with scarce on a quantity ladder and ask students to name something abundant and something scarce in their lives.
notes.va.scarce.adj: Scarce is the opposite of abundant. Ask what we do when something is scarce: share, save, and look for another source.
notes.va.ascend.v: Ascend and descend differ by only a few letters, so students mix them up. Use hand motions (up for ascend, down for descend) and a stair picture.
notes.va.descend.v: Descend is the opposite of ascend. Pair them with motions and a picture of a staircase.
notes.va.expand.v: Expand is the opposite of shrink. Note that expand does not have a perfect partner in this unit; ask students to name one (shrink).
notes.va.victory.n: Victory is winning. Pair with defeat and talk about good sportsmanship: a victory is better when winners are kind.
notes.va.defeat.n: Defeat is a noun here. Students also know it as a verb (to defeat); the unit teaches the noun. Discuss how to talk about a loss kindly.
notes.va.obvious.adj: Obvious means easy to see, but what is obvious to one reader may not be to another. Ask students to share a clue that was obvious to them.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The text says good stone was scarce, so builders carried it from far away. I do not know scarce, but I see far away. If stone were easy to find, they would not carry it. Scarce probably means hard to find. Its opposite is abundant, which fits the apples in the garden.'
discuss: Which pair in this unit is the easiest to picture? Which is the hardest?
Can a word have more than one opposite? Which words in this unit might?
misconceptions: Ancient and old mean exactly the same.
Ascend and descend mean the same because they sound alike.
Every word has one perfect opposite.
Defeat means that you are bad at something.
extend: Make a word pair poster with a picture for each word in the pair.
Write a short story about a victory and a defeat using ancient and modern settings.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Two days later, say one word from a pair and ask students to give the partner. Revisit spacious, cramped, and timid by asking which unit pairs describe a place or a person.

frames: Food is abundant in ___, but it is scarce in ___.
After the ___, the team felt ___ because ___.
wida.oral: Partner A says one word from the unit. Partner B says the opposite or a word that means almost the same and gives a short sentence.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (antiguo, escaso, derrota) are not reviewed by a native speaker.
Expand has no matching opposite in the unit (shrink is used as an outside antonym); confirm that the grouping under how much there is works for students.
The castle details in the passage are an invented but plausible scenario; no real castle or date is claimed.
